newsitem.title: GERMANY: German post workers protest against monopoly end.
newsitem.headline: German post workers protest against monopoly end.

text.p: More than 20,000 German postal workers converged on Bonn in a convoy of buses on Monday to protest against plans by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government for far-reaching postal liberalisation.

The demonstrators gathered at the headquarters of Kohl's junior coalition partner Free Democrats (FDP), who have called for ending the postal monopoly as soon as possible, and follow work stoppages at post offices in 52 cities last week.

Postal Minister Wolfgang Boetsch, highlighting a conflict between Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and liberal free-marketeers in the FDP, said the post office should keep its letter monopoly for another five years.

Boetsch told German radio that full competition for parcels should be started on January 1, 1998, but added that the post office should keep its monopoly on letters under 350 grammes for a five-year transition period ahead of full competition.
He said he wanted the post office to maintain its monopoly in this area because of the costs of getting the post office, which became Deutsche Post AG in 1995, ready for competition.
If the monopoly was not maintained beyond 1998 then large job losses would result and the tax payer would have to bear the burden of redundancy costs, he said.

But free-market advocates within the FDP and some large German companies that want to offer postal services are putting Kohl under pressure to retract earlier plans to grant the post office a five-year exclusive operator licence.

Moreover, the part of the market reserved for Deutsche Post, which could begin to be privatised next year, could be limited to letters weighing up to 100 grammes, and not the 350 grammes initially envisaged.

The Bonn government is due to discuss on Tuesday a draft law that would sweep aside the centuries-old monopoly set up by the Thurn and Taxis aristocracy which laid the basis for modern postal delivery in the 17th century.

The Deutsche Postgewerkschaft union (DPG) said around 20,000 demonstrators had arrived to attend the rally, which was due to march to the Post Ministry to hand in 300,000 post cards from supporters of "a modern, reliable post office for all."
The DPG said the Bonn plans would lead to a "poorer, scaled-down, and more expensive postal service".
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said in a statement it was on the side of postal workers and their customers.
"Changes in the postal system must not be borne on the backs of postal workers," the SPD said.

Post office counters in 52 German towns closed early on Saturday as some 8,000 postal workers continued work stoppages in protest at the planned end to the monopoly, which the DPG says could put tens of thousands of existing jobs at risk.

The DPG fears the new postal law will open the market up to "cherry-picking", in which rival operators will be able to operate in the most lucrative parts of the market, ignoring the least attractive market segments.
